The forgotten station. A relic of a bygone era, a reminder of the intricate network of railways that once crisscrossed the country. I stood at the edge of the platform, the wind whispering secrets in my ear, as I gazed out at the worn cobblestones that led nowhere. The station itself was a testament to a time when steam engines rumbled into town, disgorging weary travelers and postal workers. A time when the very notion of a remote station was a luxury.

To my left stood a small, rusted sign, once proudly bearing the station's name: Ashwood Junction. Now, it hung crookedly, as if swaying to an invisible breeze. I wondered what had been stored on these tracks – cargo bound for the interior, livestock, perhaps, or even the fleeting visage of a migrant worker.

Beyond the platform, the setting sun cast long shadows across the rural expanse. I noticed the skeleton of a rusting water tower, its metal skin encrusted with years of grime and lichen. Beneath it, a nearby sprout pushed its way through the cracked concrete, unwavering in its determination. Nature seemed to be reclaiming this forgotten place, slowly eating away at the remains of a bygone age.

As the sky deepened into a rich turquoise, I began to move towards the train tracks, exploring the makeshift satchel slung over my shoulder. Inside, I had stashed my sketchbook, switched with graphite pencils and half-finished paintings. I loved approaching unknown landscapes, witnessing how the light danced upon forms and textures, and capturing those fleeting moments of beauty on paper.

This trip had been a peculiar craving, especially since Dad had pointed out an obscure blog I'd stumbled upon months ago. David Brownson, a codgerly English artist, had spent the last decade rambling along these abandoned lines, scribing watercolors and fragments of journalling the people and scenes they met. Brownson reveled in receiving classroom-quality rail handouts, whiskers brushing against scribblings on honor-bound coaches.
